lead: A sensor turns a physical quantity into an electrical signal; an actuator turns an electrical signal into motion, heat or light. The microcontroller reads sensors and commands actuators. Signal conditioning shapes a raw sensor output for an ADC or GPIO pin. A driver lets a weak pin switch a coil, lamp or motor that needs far more current.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for pin current limits, 3.5 for duty cycle, and 3.6 for ADC input.

sections.h3: Input side: sensors and signal conditioning

blocks.text: A sensor converts a physical quantity into an electrical one. The MCU cannot read resistance; it reads a voltage on an ADC pin (3.6) or a logic level on a GPIO pin (3.1). Signal conditioning makes the sensor output fit that input.

items: LDR: resistance falls from about 1 MΩ in darkness to a few hundred ohms in bright light; a fixed series resistor forms a divider.
NTC thermistor: resistance falls as temperature rises. The curve is non-linear, so accurate readings need a lookup table or the beta formula.
Hall sensor: a logic output that flips near a magnet. Most are open-collector and need a pull-up. Used to count shaft or wheel rotations.
HC-SR04 ultrasonic: a 10 µs trigger pulse starts a sound burst; the echo pin stays high for the round trip.

blocks.where: V_out is the divider output in volts to the ADC pin; V_cc is the supply in volts; R_sensor is the sensor resistance in ohms from V_cc to the output node; R_fixed is the resistor in ohms from the output node to ground. Bright light lowers R_sensor, so V_out rises.
d is distance in metres; v is the speed of sound, about 343 m/s at 20 °C; t is the echo pulse width in seconds. The 2 covers the outbound and return path. At 343 m/s, 1 cm costs about 58 µs.

blocks.text: A push button is the simplest sensor: one side to the pin, the other to ground, plus a 10 kΩ pull-up to 3.3 V. Released, the pin reads 1; pressed, 0. Contacts bounce for 5–20 ms, so debounce: read, wait 10 ms, read again, and accept the value only when both reads agree.

sections.h3: Output side: the pin drives a transistor, not the load

blocks.text: A GPIO pin sources or sinks a few milliamperes — often 4 mA guaranteed and 20 mA absolute maximum. A 5 V relay coil draws 80 mA; a small DC motor draws 500 mA. Wiring either to a pin destroys the output driver. The pin supplies a control current; a transistor supplies the load current.

In a low-side switch the emitter goes to ground, the collector to the load, and the other end of the load to the supply. A logic 1 on the base turns the transistor on and pulls the load's lower end down to about 0.2 V, written V_CE(sat). A logic 0 turns it off.
I_B = I_C ÷ β,   R_B = (V_pin − V_BE) ÷ I_B
blocks.where: I_C is the load current in amperes; β (hFE) is the transistor's DC current gain from its datasheet, a pure number; I_B is the base current in amperes; V_pin is the GPIO high voltage in volts; V_BE is the base-emitter drop, about 0.7 V for a silicon BJT; R_B is the base resistor in ohms.

blocks.text: A relay coil is an inductor. At switch-off the coil current cannot stop instantly; the coil generates V = L·di/dt, a spike of hundreds of volts at the collector, and the transistor breaks down. A 1N4007 across the coil — cathode to the +5 V end, anode to the collector — gives that current a path and clamps the spike to about 0.7 V above the supply. Leaving it out is the most common way to kill a driver.

For a mains load the relay contact already isolates the mains from the coil side. An optocoupler such as the PC817 adds a second barrier between the pin and the driver transistor. A MOC3021 with a triac switches mains with no relay at all. For several relays, a ULN2003 packs seven Darlington pairs with the flyback diodes already inside.

A DC motor reverses when the supply polarity reverses. Four switches in an H-bridge allow either polarity: close top-left with bottom-right for one direction, top-right with bottom-left for the other. Never close both switches on one side — that is shoot-through, a direct short from supply to ground. The L293D has protection diodes built in; a bare L298N needs external fast-recovery diodes across its outputs.

Speed comes from PWM on the enable pin (3.5). The motor sees the average voltage, so 50% duty from a 12 V supply gives roughly 6 V across it, about half speed. A few kHz is fine where noise does not matter; push above 20 kHz and the switching is inaudible.

A stepper moves in fixed steps — 1.8° per step is 200 steps per revolution — and holds position when stopped. A unipolar four-phase motor (ULN2003) cannot reverse a coil, so energise the phases in order A, B, C, D, or two at a time as AB, BC, CD, DA. A bipolar two-winding motor (A4988 or H-bridge) can reverse current: the full-step order is A+, B+, A−, B−, often written A, B, A′, B′. Energise them wrongly and the rotor only vibrates. The driver IC carries the coil currents; the MCU sends only step and direction pulses.

A BLDC motor has three windings and no brushes. An electronic speed controller (ESC) switches them in the right order, using three Hall sensors or the back-EMF to find the rotor angle. Many ESCs accept a 1–2 ms pulse repeating at 50 Hz.

spec.title: Sensor input and actuator drive
spec.aria: Block diagram with a sensor going through conditioning to an ADC or GPIO, and an MCU driving a transistor base through a 2.7 kilo-ohm resistor to a relay coil and load, with a flyback diode across the coil.

examples.question: A 5 V relay coil draws 80 mA. It is switched by an NPN transistor with β = 100 and V_BE = 0.7 V. The driving GPIO pin outputs 3.3 V when high and can source at most 4 mA. Find the base current, the base resistor and the nearest standard value, and state the protection component needed.
steps: Collector current: I_C = 80 mA = 0.080 A. The coil resistance sets it (5 V ÷ 80 mA = 62.5 Ω); the transistor only carries it.
Base current: I_B = I_C ÷ β = 0.080 ÷ 100 = 0.8 mA, well inside the 4 mA the pin can source.

3.3 kΩ gives 2.6 ÷ 3300 = 0.788 mA — the rounding goes the wrong way. The next E12 value down, 2.7 kΩ, gives 2.6 ÷ 2700 = 0.96 mA. Better still, compute I_B from hFE(min) and multiply by an overdrive factor of 2–3 so the transistor sits hard in saturation.

Protection: a 1N4007 across the coil, cathode to +5 V and anode to the collector, clamps the switch-off spike. The 80 mA flows from the 5 V supply through the coil and collector; the pin carries only the base current.
examples.answer: R_B = 2.7 kΩ gives I_B ≈ 0.96 mA, and a 1N4007 flyback diode across the coil protects the transistor.
examples.check:
Vpin = 3.3
Vbe = 0.7
Ic_mA = 80.0
beta = 100
Ib_mA = Ic_mA / beta
Rb = (Vpin - Vbe) / (Ib_mA / 1000)
Ib_actual_mA = (Vpin - Vbe) / 2700 * 1000
print(Ib_mA)
print(Rb)
print(round(Ib_actual_mA, 3))

examples.question: An HC-SR04 ultrasonic module sends a trigger pulse. The echo pin stays high for 580 µs. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. Find the distance to the object.
steps: Distance = half the path = 0.19894 ÷ 2 = 0.09947 m = 9.95 cm.
examples.answer: The object is about 9.95 cm away, roughly 10 cm.
examples.check:
v = 343
t = 580e-6
d = v * t / 2
print(round(d, 5))

traps: Connecting a relay coil or motor straight to a GPIO pin. The pin is rated for a few milliamperes, the coil needs 80 mA and a motor hundreds; the output driver burns.
Leaving out the flyback diode across a coil, or fitting it the wrong way round. Anode at +5 V makes it conduct whenever the transistor is on, shorting the coil.
Confusing coil ratings with contact ratings. A relay marked 5 V, 80 mA coil and 230 V, 5 A contacts describes two separate circuits; the MCU only ever sees the first.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a flyback diode in a relay driver?
quiz.a: It gives the coil's stored current a path when the transistor turns off, clamping the inductive spike to about 0.7 V above the supply and protecting the transistor.

quiz.q: Explain why a microcontroller pin cannot drive a 5 V, 80 mA relay coil directly.
quiz.a: The pin is rated for about 4 mA guaranteed, 20 mA absolute maximum. 80 mA exceeds that, so the small output transistor inside the pin overheats and the pin or its port is destroyed. A buffer transistor carries the 80 mA; the pin supplies only the base current.

quiz.q: A 12 V relay coil draws 60 mA. The switching transistor has β = 50 and V_BE = 0.7 V. The GPIO high is 3.3 V. Find the base resistor and the nearest standard value.
An HC-SR04 echo pulse lasts 580 µs and the speed of sound is 343 m/s. Find the distance.
quiz.a: Path = 343 × 580 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.19894 m. Distance = path ÷ 2 = 0.09947 m ≈ 9.95 cm, close to the 58 µs-per-cm rule of thumb.

quiz.q: A stepper motor buzzes and vibrates but does not rotate. Driver and supply are fine. Give two likely causes and the fix.
quiz.a: The energisation sequence is wrong for the motor type: a unipolar four-phase motor needs A, B, C, D or AB, BC, CD, DA; a bipolar motor needs A+, B+, A−, B−. Correct the order. Or the step rate is faster than the motor can follow at that load, so it stalls and slips back; add a start-up ramp. A shorted coil gives the same symptom.

beyond: Industrial sensors often use a 4–20 mA current loop, which ignores voltage drop on long cables. Gate driver ICs such as the IR2110 drive MOSFET half-bridges in inverters. Smart sensors with I2C outputs, such as the BME280, move the conditioning inside the package.
